extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / Fellows of the Royal Society and interested literate public (17th-century natural historians, botanists, mineralogists, miners)
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and extracting practical identification criteria and procedural methods from 17th-century natural history / scientific journal reports (botany, mineralogy, pearl-fishing, mining, metallurgy). Useful for evaluating field reports or reproducing described techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearl-bearing shell appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The shells that have the best pearls are wrinkled, twisted, or bunched, and not smooth and equal as those that have none."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shell exterior morphology as an indicator: wrinkling/twisting/bunching suggests the shell likely contained pearls; smooth, regular shells usually have none. Note also that crafty people may conceal pearls by opening shells under water and putting pearls in their mouths or otherwise hiding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearl-fishing timing and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the warm months, before harvest is ripe, while the rivers are low and clear, the poor people go into the water and take them up, some with their toes, some with wooden tongs, and some by putting a sharpened stick into the opening of the shell."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best time: warm months when rivers are low and clear (makes shells visible). Techniques: manual picking with toes, wooden tongs, or inserting a sharpened stick into the shell opening. Yield expectation: about 1 shell in 100 may have a pearl, and of those pearls not above 1 in 100 be tolerably clear; nevertheless many fair merchantable pearls are offered each summer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearl location and formation (anatomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The part where the pearl lies is in the toe or lesser end, at the extremity of the gut, and out of the body of the fish, between the two films or skins that line the shell. I believe that this pearl answers to the stone in other animals, and certainly like that increases by several crusts, growing over one another."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locating pearls: inspect the lesser/inner end (toe) between the lining films. Formation: pearls accrete by successive crusts; compression (pinching in a vice) will crack upper coats. Pearls may be cast off and later absent in shells that once bore them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner-shell indicators of (absence of) pearls
rubrics_metrics.description: "The insides of the shells are of an oriental and pearly colour and substance, like a flat pearl, especially when first opened; and I am informed, that in some shells, under the first coat, lies a liquor very orient and clear, which moves on the pressure of the finger, but that such a muscle never has a pearl."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observing inner layers: a pearly interior is typical, but presence of a clear, movable liquor under the first coat indicates that that muscle (shell) never has a pearl—use internal characteristics as diagnostic for presence/absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calamine (lapis calaminaris) site-selection
rubrics_metrics.description: "They always dig for it upon, or near the hills; for they expect none in those grounds which have no communication with hills."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target prospecting near hills; surface indicators (water colour, grass withering, taste) unreliable. To find a vein, dig a trench as deep as the rocks across the suspected course (trenches generally north–south while courses usually lie east–west).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calamine seam orientation and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: "The courses usually lying from east to west, or at 6 o'clock, as their term is. Though this is not always the case; for sometimes the courses, seams, or rakes, as they call them, lie at 9 o'clock, and sometimes are perpendicular, which they call the high time of the day, or 12 o'clock, and these courses they esteem the best."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prospecting, consider typical seam orientations (E–W / '6 o'clock') but remain alert for variations (9 o'clock, vertical). Vertical seams ('12 o'clock') are held preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calamine and host-earth appearance as quality indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: "The colour of the earth where calamine lies, is generally a yellow grit, but sometimes black; ... Calamine itself is of several colours, some white, some reddish, some greyish, some blackish, which is counted the best; but when this is broken it is of several colours."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use host-earth colour (often yellow grit, sometimes black) and calamine colour (blackish preferred) as heuristics for identification and judging quality; note variable particle sizes (from dust to nut-size) and occasional presence of 'eyes' of lead within calamine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underground ventilation and safety in reworked mines
rubrics_metrics.description: "In old works, which are those that have been forsaken, and afterwards wrought again, damps and stenches sometimes arise, but never in new works; which damps arise from the neglect of those workmen that do not carry air along with them, which is done by air-shafts, as in lead-mines."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety practice: provide ventilation (air-shafts) when reworking old workings to avoid poisonous damps/stenches; neglecting ventilation causes hazardous air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calamine washing ('huddling') procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: "They inclose a small piece of ground with boards or turfs, through which a clear stream of water runs; within this inclosure they shovel the calamine, with the rest of the impure and earthy parts, which parts are carried away by the running water ... they often turn it, that the water passing through may wash it the better; ... they afterwards put the smaller parts ... into sieves made of strong wire at the bottom; and these sieves, with the calamine, lead, and the remainder of the earthy, sparry, and stony parts, which the water could not wash away, they often dip and shake up and down in a large tub of water, by which means the parts of the lead mixed among the calamine sink, or pitch down to the bottom of the sieves, being the heaviest, the parts of the calamine in the middle, and the other sparry, stony, and trashy parts rise up to the top; which as they rise they skim off and throw among the rest of the rubbish: then they take off the calamine, and lastly the lead."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stepwise density-separation technique: use running-water enclosure, repeated turning, coarse raking, wire sieves for finer material, and dip-shake tubs to allow gravitational separation (lead sinks, calamine intermediate, trash floats) followed by manual picking on boards. Implement sieving and multiple washing stages to maximize recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calamine calcining and finishing process
rubrics_metrics.description: "They carry it to the oven, which is much larger than a baker's oven, ... they cast in their coals into a hearth made on one side of the oven, which is divided from it by a hem or partition, made open at the top, whereby the flame of the fire passes over, and so heats and bakes the calamine. They let it lay in the oven for 4 or 5 hours, the fire burning all the while, according to the strength of the calamine... and while it continues in the oven, they turn it several times with long iron coal-rakes; when it is sufficiently burnt, baked, and dried, they beat it to a powder with long iron hammers, like mallets, on a thick plank, picking out what stones they find among it; so that at last the calamine is reduced to dust, and then it is fit for sale."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calcine for multiple hours (4–5) with indirect flame over a partitioned hearth, turn repeatedly to ensure even heating, then comminute by hammering and hand-pick residual stones to produce saleable calamine dust. Adjust time according to ore 'strength'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calamine medicinal/veterinary uses
rubrics_metrics.description: "The dust of calamine it seems conduces much to the curing of sore eyes; and that it is frequently used for taking films off the eyes of horses and other beasts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorded local medicinal/veterinary application: powdered calamine used for ocular ailments and removing films from animal eyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lottery expected-value resolution (arithmetical paradox)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A lot at either of them being truly worth just 8 pence, viz. the 6th part of 3 times 16 pence, or twice 2 shillings, the disadvantage must be the very same in both cases, that is, the gamester pays a shilling for a lot that is worth only 8 pence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate apparent paradoxes in odds, compute the true monetary value (expected value) of a lot; comparing price paid to true worth reveals the identical disadvantage across differently-stated odds. Use arithmetic of expected returns to resolve seeming contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iron-stone types and iron quality descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: "They have several sorts of iron-stone, and of different natures; for some make cold-short iron, such as is brittle, when it is cold; another sort makes red-short, such as is apt to break if it be hammered, when it is of a dark red heat, and therefore is never melted down but in mixture, and so it yields an indifferent good sort of iron."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify iron by mechanical behavior: 'cold-short' (brittle when cold) vs 'red-short' (brittle when hot). Improve quality by mixing different metals and by remelting sow-metal over again; use of turf (charcoal type/fuel) reported to improve iron quality. Choose processing routes (mixing, remelting, fuel) to mitigate brittleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Botanical description conventions for exotic plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions emphasize twig and leaf arrangement and measurements (e.g., leaves set round twig, ~4 inches long and 4/10 inch broad), indumentum ("covered over with thickest, finest, and longest white silken hair or down"), cone size and shape (cones size of cedars of Lebanon), seed morphology (shape, membranes, feathery appendages), comparisons to known species, and notes on uses and cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting exotic plant species, record: precise leaf measurements and arrangement, surface coverings (down, hair), reproductive structures (cones, flowers, seeds) with size/shape detail, comparisons to familiar taxa or prior authors, habitat and cultivation info, and practical uses (food, medicine, timber, crafts). Provide figures/plates when possible (as in the cited volumes).
